faqs.q: What is the average agronomist salary in Australia?
faqs.a: The Australian Bureau of Statistics reports average weekly earnings for full-time adult employees in professional roles at $2,083.70 per week (May 2026). For a 38-hour week, that annualises to about $108,352. However, agronomist salaries can differ based on industry, location, and experience. Some agronomists may be covered by awards like the Horticulture Award or the Professional Employees Award, which set minimum rates. Always check the relevant award or your employment contract.

faqs.q: How does casual loading affect an agronomist's pay?
faqs.a: Casual employees in the horticulture industry (including some agronomist roles) are entitled to a 25% casual loading on top of the minimum hourly rate. For example, under the Horticulture Award, a Level 1 casual adult employee earns $32.18 per hour (from 1 July 2026) compared to $25.74 for a permanent employee. The casual loading compensates for entitlements like paid leave and notice of termination. Our timesheet calculator has a checkbox to add casual loading automatically.

faqs.q: What superannuation is paid on an agronomist salary?
faqs.a: Employers must pay superannuation guarantee contributions of 12% of ordinary earnings on top of your salary, up to the maximum contribution base of $270,830 per year (2026-27). For a full-time agronomist earning $108,000, that adds about $12,960 in super annually. Super is not deducted from your pay; it's paid separately by your employer to a super fund. If you're a temporary visa holder, you may be able to access this super when you leave Australia.

bodyMarkdown:
## Agronomist Salary: Understanding Your Pay from Hourly to Annual

If you're an agronomist in Australia—whether you're advising growers, managing crop trials, or working in horticulture—you may be paid by the hour or on a salary. Converting between the two helps you compare offers and understand your entitlements. This guide explains how to calculate your annual pay from an hourly rate, what minimum rates apply, and how tax and super fit in.

### How to Calculate Annual Pay from an Hourly Rate

The standard formula for converting an hourly rate to annual gross pay is:

**Annual gross ≈ hourly rate × hours per week × 52**

For a full-time role, we assume 38 hours per week (the ordinary hours under most awards). For example, if your hourly rate is $50.00:

- $50.00 × 38 hours × 52 weeks = $98,800 per year

If you're paid fortnightly, multiply your weekly pay by 2. Using the same rate: $50.00 × 38 = $1,900 per week, so $3,800 per fortnight.

This calculation assumes the same rate every week, no unpaid overtime, no penalty rates, no allowances, and no salary sacrifice. It's a starting point for comparison.

### Award Coverage and Minimum Rates for Agronomists

Agronomists may be covered by different awards depending on their employer and duties. The Horticulture Showcase explains that employees in horticulture are usually covered by the Horticulture Award or Wine Award. Under the Horticulture Award, the minimum hourly rate for a Level 1 adult full-time employee is $25.74 (from 1 July 2026), and for a casual employee it's $32.18 (including 25% casual loading). provides full classification tables.

However, many agronomists work as professionals and may be covered by the Professional Employees Award or be award-free. The National Minimum Wage from 1 July 2026 is $26.44 per hour ($1,004.90 per week for 38 hours). Always check the Fair Work Ombudsman's Pay Calculator or your award to confirm your minimum rate.

For a benchmark, the Australian Bureau of Statistics (ABS) reports average weekly earnings for full-time adult employees in professional roles at $2,083.70 per week (May 2026). That annualises to about $108,352, which is a useful reference for an experienced agronomist salary.

### Casual Loading and Superannuation

If you work as a casual agronomist, you're entitled to a 25% casual loading on top of the minimum hourly rate. This loading replaces entitlements like annual leave, personal leave, and notice of termination. Our [casual loading](/topics/casual-loading) page explains more.

Superannuation is paid on top of your salary. From 1 July 2026, the super guarantee is 12% of ordinary earnings, up to a maximum contribution base of $270,830 per year. For a full-time agronomist earning $108,000, super adds about $12,960 annually. Super is not deducted from your pay; it's an extra contribution your employer makes to your super fund. See our [super and packaging](/topics/super-and-packaging) guide for details.

### Tax Considerations for Agronomists

Your annual gross pay is subject to income tax and the Medicare levy. The 2026-27 resident tax rates are:

- Nil on income up to $18,200
- 15% on income from $18,201 to $45,000
- 30% on income from $45,001 to $135,000
- 37% on income from $135,001 to $190,000
- 45% on income above $190,000

Plus a Medicare levy of 2% (with possible reductions for low-income earners). For a $108,000 salary, the estimated tax (including Medicare) would be around $25,000, leaving a take-home pay of about $83,000. Use our [take-home pay](/topics/take-home) calculator for a precise estimate.

### Fortnightly Pay and Budgeting

Many agronomists are paid fortnightly. To find your fortnightly gross pay, multiply your weekly pay by 2. For example, if your hourly rate is $50.00 and you work 38 hours per week:

- Weekly: $50.00 × 38 = $1,900
- Fortnightly: $1,900 × 2 = $3,800

This helps with budgeting and comparing salary offers.

### Using the Timesheet Calculator

Our [timesheet](/) tool lets you enter your base hourly rate and optionally add 25% casual loading. It calculates your weekly, fortnightly, and annual gross pay, plus estimated tax and super. Remember: the annual figure is an estimate based on 38 hours per week, 52 weeks per year. It doesn't include overtime, penalty rates, or allowances.

For more detailed award rates, check the [pay guides](/blog) or [reference tables](/data) on our site. The Fair Work Ombudsman and Fair Work Commission are the authoritative sources for minimum wages and award conditions.

### Summary

Your agronomist salary depends on your award, experience, and employment type. Use the hourly-to-annual formula to compare offers, but always verify with your employer or the Fair Work Ombudsman. Our tools help you estimate take-home pay and super, so you can plan your finances with confidence.
